claims.text: Coupling advanced free-energy sampling with machine-learning interatomic potentials can accurately determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change on melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family.
The proposed framework can determine these properties computationally efficiently.
Near-melting solid HEAs have complex, multicomponent, disordered atomic arrangements.
The machine-learning potentials will be calibrated against high-fidelity ab initio data and benchmark calorimetry.
The intended applicability covers equilibrium high-temperature conditions near melting across a broad range of HEA compositions.
Well-defined order parameters can capture the progression of atomic disorder during melting.
Tracking these order parameters mediates sampling of the solid-liquid free-energy landscape.
Sampling the full free-energy landscape of the solid-liquid transformation integrates energy barriers and changes in structural order.
This free-energy sampling yields quantitative estimates of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting.
The computed thermodynamic properties can be validated against experimental calorimetric data.
CALPHAD is an established method for practical multicomponent thermodynamic and phase-equilibrium calculations.
The proposed framework will improve accuracy relative to conventional DSC or CALPHAD methods.
Predicted melting and fusion properties may fall within 5–10% relative error.
Existing high-sensitivity DSC and first-principles molecular-dynamics results for selected HEAs provide suitable calibration references.
Insufficiently trained machine-learning potentials can limit performance for alloys with complex or metastable phase landscapes.
Order parameters that omit relevant local structural changes can prevent adequate characterization of melting.
Universal transferability of the machine-learning potentials across HEAs is uncertain.
Sampling rare-event transitions in very complex HEAs may be inefficient.
Consistent deviations greater than approximately 10% from matched experiments across a statistically significant set of HEAs would rule out the approach as an accurate predictive method.
